hooks.text: Meteors fell across North America for nine hours straight.
Shooting stars were once thought to be simple weather.
Up to 240,000 meteors lit the night sky.

title: The Meteor Storm That Created Space Science
description: A historic meteor storm over North America in 1833 launched the modern science of meteors.

beats.text: Meteors fell across North America for nine hours straight.
beats.visual: Woodcut illustration of the 1833 Leonid meteor storm over North America, Adolf Vollmy

beats.text: Eyewitnesses watched thousands of stars fall just like snow in 1833.
beats.visual: Historical engraving of people watching the 1833 Leonid meteor storm in North America

beats.text: Scientists then believed shooting stars were just weird atmospheric weather.
beats.visual: Meteoroid atmospheric entry illustration NASA, diagram showing meteor burning in atmosphere

beats.text: But Yale professor Denison Olmsted noticed something revolutionary about the storm.
beats.visual: Portrait of Yale professor Denison Olmsted, engraved portrait

beats.text: Every single meteor appeared to radiate from one specific point in Leo.
beats.visual: Diagram of meteor shower radiant point in constellation Leo, sickle of Leo diagram
queries: Sickle of Leo meteor radiant diagram

beats.text: Olmsted proved they're actually pieces of space rock, not weather.
beats.visual: Artist's concept of Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle releasing a dust trail, NASA

beats.text: This one night proved Earth was flying through a cosmic debris field.
beats.visual: Illustration of meteoroids entering Earth's atmosphere, NASA
queries: Meteoroid stream Earth orbit intersection diagram

beats.text: Modern meteor science exists today all because of that historic night.
beats.visual: Long-exposure photo of the 1966 Leonid meteor storm, Arizona

better_than_last: Incorporated the reviewer's specific phrasing for the penultimate beat to emphasize the cosmic discovery while maintaining the loop.
